titre: The Nika revolt (532), which gave birth to Hagia Sophia
accroche: In January 532, a riot by chariot-racing fans nearly overthrows Emperor Justinian and destroys part of Constantinople.
contenu_vulgarise:
In January 532, Constantinople goes up in flames over a matter of chariot races. The Blues and the Greens, the two rival factions of the hippodrome, have acquired considerable political influence in the capital of the Byzantine Empire, to the point of weighing on imperial appointments and sometimes clashing in the streets. On January 10, two men sentenced to death for violence tied to these rivalries (one Blue, the other Green) survive their hanging when the scaffold gives way under them. Monks shelter them in a church. The two factions, united for once, demand their pardon.

## From a stadium brawl to an attempted coup

On January 13, during the races held at the hippodrome, the crowd chants *Nika* (“conquer,” or “victory”) over and over, which will give the revolt its name. Within a few days, the riot spirals out of control: fires ravage the center of the city, including the basilica of Hagia Sophia built under Constantine, and the rioters proclaim a new emperor, Hypatius, nephew of a previous sovereign. Justinian, holed up in his palace, considers fleeing by sea. It is his wife, Empress Theodora, a former actress turned sovereign, who talks him out of it: according to the historian Procopius, a witness of the time, she declares before the imperial council that those who have worn the crown must never survive its loss, refusing to flee while the throne is under threat.

Justinian stays. His generals, Belisarius and Mundus, surround the rioters massed in the hippodrome and massacre them there: Procopius puts forward a figure of thirty thousand dead, an order of magnitude that modern historians consider plausible given the scale of the destruction reported. Hypatius is executed.

## A disaster turned monument

Barely forty days after the fire that destroyed the old basilica, Justinian launches, on February 23, 532, the construction of a building without equivalent: a dome more than thirty meters in diameter, designed by the mathematician Anthemius of Tralles and the geometer Isidore of Miletus, and built by more than ten thousand workers. The new Hagia Sophia is consecrated on December 27, 537: less than six years after the riot that nearly overthrew the empire. The worst crisis of Justinian's reign thus produced his most lasting monument: it remains, nearly fifteen centuries later, one of the largest religious buildings ever built without a load-bearing metal structure.

carte.punch: A riot by chariot-racing fans nearly overthrew Justinian, and gave us Hagia Sophia.
carte.idee: In January 532, a rivalry between hippodrome factions degenerates into a revolt in Constantinople: fires, thirty thousand dead according to Procopius, a rival proclaimed emperor. Saved by the refusal of his wife Theodora to flee, Justinian crushes the revolt and builds, in less than six years, Hagia Sophia.

quiz.question: What convinces Justinian not to flee Constantinople during the Nika revolt of 532?
choix: The arrival of reinforcements from Antioch
A personal intervention by the Persian emperor Khosrow I
The refusal of his wife Theodora to survive the loss of the throne
The pope's promise to recognize his legitimacy
quiz.explication: According to Procopius, a witness of the time, Empress Theodora refused to flee, declaring that those who have worn the crown must never survive its loss: a speech that supposedly decided Justinian to stay and retake the city by force.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What cry chanted by the crowd at the hippodrome gives the 532 revolt its name?
choix: Nika, that is, conquer or victory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On January 13, 532, the crowd chants Nika over and over, conquer or victory, during the races at the hippodrome, which will give the entire revolt its name.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which of Justinian's generals surround and massacre the rioters gathered in the hippodrome?
choix: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus
The priests of the basilica of Hagia Sophia
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The generals Belisarius and Mundus surround the rioters massed in the hippodrome and massacre them there, an episode that Procopius estimates at about thirty thousand dead.
